extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (agents/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing judicial-exception analyses under 35 U.S.C. §101, including (1) the 'markedly different characteristics' product-of-nature analysis for nature-based products and (2) the Alice/Mayo Step 2B search for an inventive concept. Intended to direct examiner claim comparisons, characteristic selection, and evaluation of additional elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis compares the nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state. Markedly different characteristics can be expressed as the product’s structure, function, and/or other properties, and are evaluated based on what is recited in the claim on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the analysis indicates that a nature-based product limitation does not exhibit markedly different characteristics, then that limitation is a product of nature exception. If the analysis indicates that a nature-based product limitation has markedly different characteristics, then that limitation is not a product of nature exception. If the nature-based product is naturally occurring, no analysis is necessary because it by definition falls under the product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state to compare against the nature-based product limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counterpart should be the closest natural product from which the claimed product was derived (e.g., a chemical derivative is compared to the natural chemical). Use the closest natural counterpart even if it is a subset (e.g., a gene vs. the whole chromosome). When multiple possible counterparts exist, select the counterpart most closely related based on examiner expertise; for combinations with no natural counterpart, compare to the individual natural components (e.g., species in a bacterial mixture). If a claim is rejected, as a best practice identify the selected counterpart in the Office action to clarify the record and assist applicant response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate counterpart with adjacent naturally occurring material
rubrics_metrics.description: The selected counterpart should be in its natural state but should not be confused with other material that may occur naturally with or adjacent to the counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For a claimed nucleic acid derived from gene B, compare to gene B itself, not the whole chromosome. For a single-stranded primer derived from double-stranded nucleic acid C, compare to the corresponding sense strand only.

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiple counterparts exist, compare to the closest(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is no single closest natural counterpart (e.g., product created from multiple donors or combined components), the examiner should select the most closely related counterpart(s) for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examiner expertise to pick the closest counterpart(s) (e.g., donor breeds in a cloned animal). For mixtures not found in nature, compare to the individual species/components. Cite relevant precedent (Roslin, Chakrabarty, Funk Bros., Ambry) when applying this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify appropriate characteristics for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the characteristics of the claimed nature-based product to compare to the counterpart; appropriate characteristics must be possessed by the claimed product and are determined from the claim language and its broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics may be explicitly recited in the claim or apparent from the broadest reasonable interpretation (e.g., chemical name, 'isolated gene B'). Unclaimed characteristics cannot be relied upon. Consider what the claim defines and what is encompassed by that definition when identifying characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of characteristics to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate characteristics can be expressed as the nature-based product’s structure, function, and/or other properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting types courts consider include: biological or pharmacological functions/activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype (functional and structural characteristics); and structure and form (chemical, genetic or physical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of biological or pharmacological functions/activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific biological/pharmacological characteristics courts have considered when assessing marked difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: (i) protein-encoding information of a nucleic acid (Myriad); (ii) ability of complementary nucleotide sequences to bind (Ambry); (iii) properties/functions of bacteria such as ability to infect certain plants (Funk Bros.); (iv) ability to degrade hydrocarbons (Chakrabarty); (v) vitamin C's ability to prevent/treat scurvy (King).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of chemical and physical properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical/physical properties considered in marked-difference analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: alkalinity of a compound (Parke-Davis) and ductility/malleability of metals (Marden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of phenotypic characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenotypic (functional/structural) features courts consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include shape, size, color, and behavior of an organism (Roslin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of structure and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural/genetic/physical forms used in comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: physical presence of plasmids in a cell (Chakrabarty); chemical form such as nonsalt/crystalline substances (Parke-Davis); nucleotide sequence of DNA (Myriad); genetic makeup/genotype of a cell or organism (Roslin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating whether characteristics are 'markedly different'
rubrics_metrics.description: A characteristic must be changed as compared to nature and cannot be an inherent/innate characteristic of the naturally occurring counterpart or an incidental change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be markedly different, applicant must have caused the claimed product to possess at least one characteristic different from the counterpart. If there is no change in any characteristic, the claim lacks markedly different characteristics and is a product-of-nature exception. If there is a change and it was produced by applicant’s efforts/influences, the change will generally be considered markedly different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of characteristics that establish marked difference (case examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Court examples illustrating characteristics judged sufficiently changed to avoid the product-of-nature exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chakrabarty: genetically modified bacterium with additional plasmids and expanded ability to degrade multiple hydrocarbons (changed function and structure). Myriad cDNA: cDNA differs structurally (exons-only nucleotide sequence) from naturally occurring DNA even if it encodes same protein.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of characteristics that do NOT establish marked difference (case examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Court examples where changes were incidental/not enough, or where claimed differences were unclaimed/innate and thus insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad isolated genes: isolation-induced incidental structural changes (loss of covalent bonds) were not enough because genes remained otherwise identical. Ambry primers: single-stranded primers corresponded exactly to natural sequences and exploited innate binding function of DNA; thus lacked markedly different characteristics. Roslin clones: clones were genetic replicas; unclaimed phenotypic differences did not make them markedly different. Marden: inherent ductility was not given by applicant and thus not markedly different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for an inventive concept (Alice/Mayo Step 2B – overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: After determining a claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon), determine whether the claim integrates the exception into an 'inventive concept' so that the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventive concept cannot be furnished by the unpatentable judicial exception itself. It must be an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception and be sufficient to ensure the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more. Consider additional elements both individually and as an ordered combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of claim elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating additional elements requires assessing both their individual contribution and their combined effect to determine whether they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although an element may not be significantly more on its own, a non-conventional, non-generic arrangement of individually known elements may provide an inventive concept (e.g., BASCOM; CellzDirect). Claims must be considered as a whole (Diehr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate inventive concept inquiry with novelty/non-obviousness (§102/§103)
rubrics_metrics.description: The search for an inventive concept under §101 is distinct from novelty (§102) and obviousness (§103) inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of novelty or an obviousness determination under §§102/103 does not determine whether additional elements are 'well-understood, routine, conventional' for §101 purposes. Courts have rejected substituting §§102/103/112 inquiries for the §101 analysis (Mayo, Intellectual Ventures, Synopsys).

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations that courts have found to qualify as 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that courts have found, when recited with a judicial exception, to qualify as 'significantly more' (non-exhaustive list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes (i) improvements to functioning of a computer (DDR Holdings example); (ii) improvements to any other technology/technical field (Diehr thermocouple example); (iii) applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine arranged in a particular way (Eibel/Fourdrinier example); (iv) effecting a transformation/reduction of an article to a different state or thing (Diehr rubber example); (v) adding specific limitations other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (BASCOM non-conventional arrangement); (vi) other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the exception to a technological environment (Classen immunization example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of limitations found NOT to be 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations courts have held insufficient to transform a claim directed to a judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: (i) merely adding the words 'apply it' or equivalent instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer (Alice); (ii) appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities at a high level of generality (generic computer implementation) (Alice); (iii) adding insignificant extra-solution activity such as mere data gathering (CyberSource); (iv) generally linking the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (Bilski, Parker v. Flook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality/tangibility of additional elements is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physical implementation or tangibility is not, by itself, an inventive concept; nor is the absence of physicality dispositive against eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that a computer is a tangible machine does not automatically render a claim patent-eligible; courts have warned that counting tangibility alone would let applicants claim any principle by reciting a computer. Conversely, improvements that are not defined by physical components can still be eligible if they improve an existing technological process (Enfish, McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: How courts conduct the Step 2B analysis (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative stepwise approach courts have used in analyzing inventive concept under Alice and related cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Alice): identify additional claim elements (hardware/software steps), consider them individually (are they well-understood, routine, conventional?), then consider them as an ordered combination (do they add something substantially more?). Example (BASCOM): district court identified elements as generic, but Federal Circuit emphasized considering the unconventional arrangement of components together to find an inventive concept.
